extracted.intended_audience: corporate counsel, SEC reporting officers, general counsels, CFOs, and compliance professionals at public companies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on when to file SEC Form 8-K for specific reportable events, what disclosure is required for each item, and practical tips for preparing and timing 8-Ks (including cybersecurity incident materiality assessments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form 8-K item structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Each reportable event review is divided into three parts: “An 8-K Is Required If” (events that trigger an Item), “Required Disclosure” (what must be included in the Form 8-K), and “Practice Tips” (suggestions for complying and implementing disclosure controls and procedures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing an 8-K for any Item, follow the three-part structure and remember that Rule 12b-20 and Rule 10b-5 require inclusion of other material information necessary to make required disclosures not misleading. Use the Practice Tips to refine content and filing approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 12b-20 / §10(b) / Rule 10b-5 anti‑misleading obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to item-specific requirements, each Form 8-K must include all other material information, if any, that is necessary to make the required disclosure, in light of the circumstances under which it is made, not misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies must consider whether additional context or facts beyond the item’s checklist are necessary to avoid a misleading statement or omission. This obligation can require disclosure of quantitative and qualitative impacts or explanatory detail even if not explicitly listed under an Item.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of §10(b)/Rule 10b-5 safe harbor and impact on Form S-3 eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: For each Form 8-K Item, determine whether the §10(b)/Rule 10b-5 safe harbor applies and whether the Item affects Form S-3 eligibility (the Guide’s table lists applicability per Item).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the item-by-item table (shows, for example, Item 1.01: Yes safe harbor; Item 1.03: No safe harbor) to assess potential securities-law exposure and whether an 8-K filing will affect registration form eligibility. Treat these determinations as part of the filing analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 1.01 — Entry into a Material Definitive Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: An 8-K is required if the company has entered into a “material definitive agreement” not made in the ordinary course of business, entered into an amendment to such an agreement that is material, or succeeded as a party to such an agreement by assumption or assignment (other than in a merger/acquisition). A “material definitive agreement” provides obligations or rights that are material and enforceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required disclosure: date of agreement/amendment; identity of parties; brief description of other material relationships between the company (or affiliates) and any parties; brief description of terms and conditions material to the company (including rights/obligations, duration, termination provisions). Guidance includes: apply Regulation S-K Item 601(b)(10) to determine “not in the ordinary course” (examples: company substantially dependent on the agreement; acquisition/sale of property/plant/equipment >15% of fixed assets; material lease; director/officer as party). Exclusions: compensatory plans/contracts covering directors/executive officers and certain equity plans adopted without stockholder approval are not “material definitive agreements” for Item 1.01 (but may be reportable elsewhere). Practice Tips (A–D) advise: always include a brief summary in the Form 8-K body even if the agreement is filed as an exhibit; when appropriate, consider filing the full agreement as an exhibit; identify planned redactions in advance; for business combination agreements, disclose common material terms (consideration, committed financing, post-closing ownership/management structure, material conditions to closing, anticipated filing/closing timeframes); redaction and exhibit-filing considerations (SEC staff encourages filing business combination agreements as exhibits where feasible); treat oral agreements as covered (provide a written description when filed as an exhibit); immaterial amendments need not trigger 8-K but may still need to be filed as an exhibit to Form 10‑Q/10‑K; assume filing required even if agreement is subject to significant conditions (e.g., board approval).

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 1.02 — Termination of a Material Definitive Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: An 8-K is required if a material definitive agreement not made in the ordinary course of business is terminated and such termination is material to the company (but not required for ordinary expiration or full performance). “Material definitive agreement” has same meaning as Item 1.01.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required disclosure: date of termination; identity of parties; brief description of other material relationships between the company (or affiliates) and any parties; brief description of terms/conditions material to the company; description of material circumstances surrounding the termination; any material early termination penalties incurred. Practice Tips: filing required regardless of which party triggers termination; do not file based solely on negotiations unless termination has occurred; receipt of a termination notice under the agreement triggers filing even if termination occurs later (consider filing and explaining if company believes notice is invalid); when drafting agreements avoid using a termination notice to start a cure period (receipt of notice triggers 8‑K); renewal/non‑renewal notice rules (sending a non‑renewal notice may trigger an Item 1.02 filing within four business days; automatic renewal typically does not require a new Item 1.01 filing); keep the Form 10‑K exhibit list current to avoid unnecessary Item 1.02 filings; termination by a subsidiary is reportable if material to the company; termination of compensatory arrangements is excluded from Item 1.02 but may trigger Item 5.02(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 1.03 — Bankruptcy or Receivership
rubrics_metrics.description: An 8-K is required if a receiver, fiscal agent or similar officer is appointed for the company (or parent) under bankruptcy or other proceedings placing substantially all assets or business under court/government authority, or if an order confirming a plan of reorganization/arrangement/liquidation is entered by a court/governmental authority having supervision over substantially all of the assets or business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required disclosure for bankruptcy: name/identification of the proceeding; identity of the court or governmental authority; date jurisdiction was assumed; identity of the receiver/fiscal agent/similar officer and appointment date. For a reorganization/arrangement/liquidation order: identity of the court/authority; date order confirming plan was entered; summary of material features of the plan and, per Item 9.01, a copy of the confirmed plan; number of shares/units issued and outstanding and reserved for future issuance in respect of claims/interests and aggregate totals; information on assets and liabilities as of the confirmation date or as close as practicable. Practice Tip: asset/liability information may be presented in the form furnished to the court or governmental authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 1.05 — Material Cybersecurity Incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: An 8-K is required if the company experiences a cybersecurity incident that the company determines is material. “Cybersecurity incident” = unauthorized occurrence or series of related unauthorized occurrences on or conducted through a company’s information systems that jeopardize confidentiality, integrity, or availability. “Information systems” = electronic information resources owned or used by the company (including physical/virtual infrastructure or components) organized for collection, processing, maintenance, use, sharing, dissemination, or disposition of the company’s information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Potential for delayed disclosure: US Attorney General may authorize up to 30-day delay (plus additional optional 30- and final 60-day periods in extraordinary circumstances) by notifying the SEC in writing when disclosure poses substantial risk to national security/public safety; Exchange Act Rule 0-6 and FCC CPNI rules can also permit delays (CPNI-covered companies may delay public/customer notification up to seven days after USSS/FBI notification if SEC is notified). Required disclosure: material aspects of the nature, scope, and timing of the incident; material impact or reasonably likely material impact on the company, including financial condition and results of operations. If required information is not available at filing, include a statement to that effect and file an amendment within four business days after the information becomes available or is determined. SEC staff statements (May 21, 2024 and June 20, 2024) clarify voluntary disclosure paths (e.g., Item 7.01 or 8.01) and that if an incident later becomes material the company must file Item 1.05 within four business days of materiality determination; the June statement clarifies interplay with Regulation FD and that companies can discuss incidents with counterparties or others (subject to confidentiality/reg FD rules). The staff has sought full disclosure of actual or reasonably likely material impacts and expects both quantitative and qualitative factors to be considered. Practice Tips (selected): materiality should be analyzed under traditional securities-law definition considering qualitative and quantitative factors; materiality determinations must be made without unreasonable delay; voluntary disclosure under Item 7.01 or 8.01 is permitted before materiality is determined (but Item 1.05 must be filed if later determined material); definition of “series of related unauthorized occurrences” should be viewed broadly; disclose incidents at third‑party service providers if they have a material impact on the company (but companies need only disclose what is made available to them consistent with disclosure controls); avoid disclosing technical details that would impede response or remediation (Instruction 4 to Item 1.05); consider trading-window closures while assessing materiality; use prior SEC guidance (2011 staff guidance and 2018 interpretive guidance) to inform disclosures not explicitly addressed by Item 1.05 or Item 106 of Regulation S‑K.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing materiality of cybersecurity incidents — factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Materiality of a cybersecurity incident is determined under the traditional securities-law test (substantial likelihood a reasonable shareholder would consider it important or that it would significantly alter the total mix of information). Registrants must consider both qualitative and quantitative factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considerations that will not be relevant: whether affected system was owned/operated by registrant or a third party; inability to determine full extent at time of assessment; ongoing nature of internal investigation; timing of sharing information with governmental authorities or others. Quantitative considerations: reasonably expected percentage impact on revenue due to lost sales; percentage impact on net income due to lost revenues and remediation/response/ legal/regulatory expenses (including ransom); percentage impact on total and current assets from incident-related expenses/write-downs. Qualitative considerations: relative importance of systems affected; duration of incident, detection method, readiness of response; ability to restore systems and expected integrity after restoration; nature/scope/magnitude of improperly accessed or exfiltrated information; effect on “crown-jewel” systems; reputational/brand harm; impact on supply chain and operations (including consequential harms); impact on customer relationships (near- and long-term); impact on suppliers/business partners; effect on competitive position; likelihood of regulatory action; likelihood of private litigation by affected individuals. Use both quantitative and qualitative factors in a reasoned, documented materiality assessment and make determination without unreasonable delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item 2.01 — Completion of Acquisition or Disposition of Assets
rubrics_metrics.description: An 8‑K is required when the company (or consolidated subsidiary) completes the acquisition or disposition of a significant amount of assets other than in the ordinary course of business, or a significant amount of assets constituting a real estate operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions and examples: “acquisition” includes purchase, acquisition by lease, exchange, merger, consolidation, succession or other acquisition but excludes construction/development or acquisition of materials intended for construction; “disposition” includes sale, disposition by lease, exchange, merger, consolidation, mortgage, assignment, hypothecation, abandonment, destruction, or other disposition (an indefinite closing of part of a company’s facilities coupled with a write-down of assets in excess of 10% constitutes an “other disposition” reportable under this item). Acquisition/disposition of securities is treated as indirect acquisition/disposition of the assets represented if it results in control of such assets. (See SEC CDI Question 205.04 and Division of Corp. Finance Financial Reporting Manual section cited.)
